      "content": "## Table of Contents[#](https://www.javathinking.com#table-of-contents)

## What is HikariCP?[#](https://www.javathinking.com#what-is-hikaricp)

HikariCP is a "zero-overhead" production-grade connection pool for Java. Developed by Brett Wooldridge, it is renowned for its speed, efficiency, and minimal resource footprint. Spring Boot adopted HikariCP as the default connection pool in version 2.0 (replacing Tomcat JDBC Pool) due to its superior performance metrics, including:

- **Low latency**: Optimized connection retrieval and release logic.
- **Small codebase**: \~130KB JAR size, reducing startup time and memory overhead.
- **Smart pooling**: Features like adaptive timeout handling and connection health checks.

HikariCP's design philosophy emphasizes "doing more with less," making it ideal for high-throughput Spring Boot applications. Central to its configuration is `maximumPoolSize`, which dictates the upper limit of concurrent database connections the pool will manage.

## Default `maximumPoolSize` in Spring Boot: A Version-Specific Breakdown[#](https://www.javathinking.com#default-maximumpoolsize-in-spring-boot-a-version-specific-breakdown)

The default value of `maximumPoolSize` in HikariCP has remained consistent across Spring Boot versions. Understanding this default is critical for proper connection pool tuning.

### 1. Spring Boot \< 2.3: Fixed Default of 10 Connections[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-spring-boot-less-than-2-3-fixed-default-of-10-connections)

Prior to Spring Boot 2.3, HikariCP's `maximumPoolSize` was **fixed at 10 connections**, regardless of the underlying hardware (e.g., CPU cores, memory) or database capacity. This static default was a safe starting point but often required manual tuning for applications with high concurrency or running on multi-core servers.

### 2. Spring Boot ≥ 2.3: Default Remains at 10[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-spring-boot-2-3-default-remains-at-10)

Starting with Spring Boot 2.3, the default `maximumPoolSize` remains **fixed at 10 connections**, consistent with earlier versions. While Spring Boot 2.3 introduced many configuration improvements, it did not change the HikariCP default pool size from 10.

#### Why Not a Dynamic Default?[#](https://www.javathinking.com#why-not-a-dynamic-default)

Unlike some connection pool parameters that auto-tune based on hardware, `maximumPoolSize` requires careful consideration of your specific database server's capacity, not just CPU cores. A one-size-fits-all formula can be misleading—database workload characteristics (query complexity, connection holding time, etc.) vary significantly across applications.

#### Customizing Based on CPU Cores (Optional)[#](https://www.javathinking.com#customizing-based-on-cpu-cores-optional)

If you want to tune `maximumPoolSize` dynamically based on CPU cores, you can configure it manually in your `application.properties`:

This SpEL expression calculates `availableProcessors() * 2 + 1` at runtime. For example, on an 8-core CPU, this yields 17 connections.

#### Examples:[#](https://www.javathinking.com#examples)

- **4-core CPU**: `4 * 2 + 1 = 9` connections.
- **8-core CPU**: `8 * 2 + 1 = 17` connections.
- **16-core CPU**: `16 * 2 + 1 = 33` connections.

Use this approach only after verifying your database can handle the increased connection load.

## Why Does This Default Exist? The Rationale Behind the Heuristic[#](https://www.javathinking.com#why-does-this-default-exist-the-rationale-behind-the-heuristic)

The default of 10 connections in Spring Boot is not arbitrary. It is rooted in performance engineering principles and real-world database behavior:

### 1. Avoiding Database Overload[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-avoiding-database-overload)

Databases have finite resources (CPU, memory, I/O). Each connection consumes database memory (e.g., for session state, query caching) and can increase lock contention. Too many connections overwhelm the database, leading to slower query execution and timeouts.

### 2. Minimizing Thread Contention[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-minimizing-thread-contention)

Java threads (and thus database connections) compete for CPU time. Excessive connections lead to frequent context switching (the OS pausing one thread to run another), which degrades performance. The `availableProcessors() * 2 + 1` formula (if you choose to use it) aligns with the "optimal thread count" heuristic, where threads ≈ 2× CPU cores to keep cores busy without excessive switching.

### 3. Balancing Throughput and Latency[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-balancing-throughput-and-latency)

A pool that is too small causes request queuing and timeouts. Too large wastes resources on idle connections. The default of 10 strikes a balance: enough connections to handle typical workloads, but not so many that the database becomes a bottleneck.

## How to Verify the Default `maximumPoolSize`[#](https://www.javathinking.com#how-to-verify-the-default-maximumpoolsize)

To confirm the active `maximumPoolSize` in your Spring Boot application, use one of these methods:

### 1. Check HikariCP Startup Logs[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-check-hikaricp-startup-logs)

HikariCP logs pool configuration on startup. Look for a line like this in your application logs (adjust log level to `INFO` if needed):

Here, `maximumPoolSize=10` confirms the default pool size.

### 2. Programmatically Inspect the Pool[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-programmatically-inspect-the-pool)

Expose the `HikariDataSource` and log its configuration. Add this to a `@Configuration` class:

On startup, this will print the active `maximumPoolSize` to the console.

### 3. Use JMX[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-use-jmx)

HikariCP exposes metrics via JMX. Use tools like JConsole or VisualVM to connect to your application and navigate to `com.zaxxer.hikari:type=HikariPool (HikariPool-1)` → Attributes → `MaximumPoolSize`.

## Impact of Over-Setting `maximumPoolSize`: Risks and Consequences[#](https://www.javathinking.com#impact-of-over-setting-maximumpoolsize-risks-and-consequences)

It's tempting to increase `maximumPoolSize` to "handle more traffic," but this often backfires. Here's why over-setting the pool size harms performance:

### 1. Database Resource Starvation[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-database-resource-starvation)

Each connection consumes database resources (memory, file descriptors, locks). For example, PostgreSQL defaults to `max_connections=100`—if your app sets `maximumPoolSize=200`, the database will reject new connections, causing `SQLTransientConnectionException`.

### 2. Increased Context Switching[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-increased-context-switching)

Too many active connections mean more threads competing for CPU. The OS spends more time switching between threads than executing useful work, reducing throughput.

### 3. Connection Contention and Timeouts[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-connection-contention-and-timeouts)

Idle connections in an over-sized pool may become stale (due to database timeouts like `wait_timeout` in MySQL). When the pool tries to reuse them, it incurs reconnection overhead, leading to slower response times.

### 4. Wasted Memory[#](https://www.javathinking.com#4-wasted-memory)

Idle connections consume JVM memory (e.g., HikariCP's `idleTimeout` defaults to 600000ms/10 minutes). An over-sized pool wastes memory on unused connections, increasing GC pressure.

### 5. Masking Underlying Issues[#](https://www.javathinking.com#5-masking-underlying-issues)

A large pool can hide bottlenecks (e.g., slow queries, unoptimized indexes). Instead of fixing the root cause, you're papering over it with more connections, leading to unsustainable scaling.

### Example: The "Too Many Connections" Disaster[#](https://www.javathinking.com#example-the-too-many-connections-disaster)

An e-commerce app sets `maximumPoolSize=200` to handle Black Friday traffic. The database (with `max_connections=150`) starts rejecting connections. Retries exacerbate the issue, causing cascading failures. Meanwhile, the app's 200 threads spend most of their time waiting for database locks, dropping throughput by 40%.

## Best Practices for Setting `maximumPoolSize`[#](https://www.javathinking.com#best-practices-for-setting-maximumpoolsize)

Follow these steps to optimize `maximumPoolSize` for your workload:

### 1. Start with the Default[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-start-with-the-default)

The default of 10 connections works for most applications. Only tune if you observe connection-related bottlenecks (e.g., `HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms`).

### 2. Monitor Pool Metrics[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-monitor-pool-metrics)

Track these HikariCP metrics to identify issues:

- `ActiveConnections`: Number of in-use connections (should stay below `maximumPoolSize`).
- `IdleConnections`: Unused connections (high values indicate over-provisioning).
- `PendingConnections`: Requests waiting for a connection (high values mean the pool is too small).

Use tools like Micrometer + Prometheus/Grafana to visualize these metrics.

### 3. Respect Database Limits[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-respect-database-limits)

Check your database's `max_connections` (e.g., `SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections'` in MySQL). Set `maximumPoolSize` to **≤ (max\_connections - reserved\_connections)** (reserve connections for admins/other apps).

### 4. Load-Test Under Realistic Traffic[#](https://www.javathinking.com#4-load-test-under-realistic-traffic)

Simulate peak load with tools like JMeter. If `PendingConnections` spike, increment `maximumPoolSize` by small steps (e.g., +5) and retest. Stop when adding connections no longer improves throughput.

### 5. Tune Complementary Settings[#](https://www.javathinking.com#5-tune-complementary-settings)

- `connectionTimeout`: Time to wait for a connection (default: 30000ms). Increase if `PendingConnections` are high but the pool isn't saturated.
- `idleTimeout`: Time to keep idle connections (default: 600000ms). Reduce for memory-constrained environments.
- `minIdle`: Minimum idle connections (default: same as `maximumPoolSize`). Lower to free resources if idle connections are high.

## Conclusion[#](https://www.javathinking.com#conclusion)

HikariCP's `maximumPoolSize` is a critical lever for Spring Boot performance, but more is not better. Spring Boot's default of 10 connections provides a safe starting point that balances throughput and database health for most applications. Over-setting the pool size leads to database overload, context switching, and wasted resources.

Optimize `maximumPoolSize` by monitoring metrics, respecting database limits, and load-testing. When in doubt, start with the default and tune incrementally. Your database (and users) will thank you.",

      "content": "HikariCP pool size should be treated as a capacity control, not a performance score. maximumPoolSize sets the upper connection limit, while minimumIdle affects how many idle connections the pool tries to maintain when configured below that maximum.

## What maximumPoolSize changes

The pool maximum includes idle and in-use connections. When every connection is in use and the pool is at its maximum, new callers wait for a connection until one is returned or the connection timeout is reached.

A higher maximum can reduce queueing only if the database can productively handle the additional concurrent work.

## How minimumIdle affects behavior

minimumIdle asks the pool to maintain a baseline of idle connections. The HikariCP project documentation notes that leaving it unset can allow fixed-size behavior based on maximumPoolSize, which is a useful starting point for many workloads.

Do not set a large idle baseline without understanding database connection costs and infrastructure limits.

## Use database capacity as a boundary

The application is not the only client of the database. Administrators, background jobs, other services and maintenance tools may share the same connection limit. Reserve operational headroom instead of allocating every possible database connection to one pool.

## Include transaction duration in sizing

Long transactions keep connections checked out for longer periods, which increases the number of concurrent connections needed for the same request rate. Reducing transaction duration can be more effective than increasing the pool.

## Validate with load tests

Start from a conservative maximum, run representative traffic, and observe throughput, latency, waiting threads and database load. Increase or decrease capacity based on evidence, not a copied formula alone.

## Next steps

Keep the configuration small, record the exact library version or source revision, and test the complete application-to-database path. For broader topics, use the [HikariCP guide library](https://hikaricp.com/blog.html) or return to the [homepage FAQ](https://hikaricp.com/index.html#faq).",
